plain: The model was tested on 6,024 customers it had never seen before.
Of every 100 customers who really missed a payment, it had warned about 35 of them.
When it gave a warning, it was right about 67 times out of 100.
Its percentages are realistic: on average it estimated 22%, and 22% actually missed.
Ranking quality is 0.76 (0.5 = coin flip, 1.0 = perfect): fair to good for this kind of data.
Trade-off: it misses many customers who later miss a payment. To catch more, lower the warning level below. You will also get more false alarms.

help.name: Missed payments caught
help.text: Recall. Of the customers who really missed a payment, the share the model had warned about. Missing them is usually the most expensive mistake.

help.name: Warnings that were right
help.text: Precision. Of the customers the model warned about, the share who really missed a payment. The rest were false alarms.

help.name: Overall correct calls
help.text: Accuracy. Share of all customers the model called right. It looks good easily: saying 'everyone will pay' would already score 78%.

help.name: Ranking quality
help.text: ROC-AUC. How well the model puts risky customers above safe ones. 0.5 = coin flip, 1.0 = perfect.

help.name: Balance score
help.text: F1 score. One number combining 'caught' and 'right'. Higher is better.

message.text: Yes. When the model says, for example, 30%, about 30 in 100 of those customers really missed a payment.
